# Recentered Formula Instruments Consider a randomized experiment in two strata of 100 units each. In stratum A each unit is treated with probability 0.8, and in stratum B with probability 0.2. Untreated units have outcome 10 in A and 0 in B, and treatment raises the outcome by 1 for everyone. In a typical draw 80 units in A and 20 in B are treated. The treated then have mean $(80 \times 11 + 20 \times 1)/100 = 9$, and the controls $(20 \times 10 + 80 \times 0)/100 = 2$. The difference in means is 7, although every effect is 1. Assignment is random, but A is treated more often and has higher outcomes anyway, and the comparison mixes the two. The usual fix is to control for the stratum. There is another way to see it. Let $D_i$ be unit $i$'s treatment and $p_i$ its assignment probability, 0.8 or 0.2. The difference $D_i - p_i$ averages zero within each stratum, so it is uncorrelated with anything fixed within a stratum, including the baseline outcome. In this draw, using $D_i - p_i$ as the instrument for $D_i$ gives exactly 1, and so does controlling for $p_i$. Many treatments have the same structure, but nobody writes the probability down. Medicaid eligibility applies a state's rules, which may be as good as random, to a person's income, which is not. Import exposure applies industry shocks to a region's industry mix. Spillover exposure applies a random assignment to the map of schools. Units with more exposure expect more treatment in every draw, as stratum A did. Here the stratum is the exposure itself, such as income or a region's industry shares. It is continuous, so no two units share one and we cannot compare within strata. The expected treatment reduces it to one number, as a propensity score does. @borusyak-hull-2023 show that the same fix works: subtract each unit's expected treatment, computed from the formula and the distribution of the shocks, or control for it. @borusyak-hull-2026 show which formula is best. We apply the result to the Bartik instrument, the China shock and spillovers in a deworming experiment. ## Formula instruments Unit $i$ has outcome $y_i$ and treatment $x_i$, with a constant effect $\beta$: $$ y_i = \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i . $$ {#eq-ri-model} The treatment is $x_i = h_i(g, w, u)$, where $h_i$ is a known function, $g$ collects the random shocks, $w$ collects predetermined variables such as income or industry shares, and $u$ collects anything else. The identifying assumption is that only the shocks are random [@borusyak-hull-2026, Assumption 1]: $$ E[\varepsilon_i \mid g, w] = E[\varepsilon_i \mid w] . $$ {#eq-ri-exog} The error may depend on $w$ in any way. Poorer people may have worse outcomes, and regions with more manufacturing may have been declining anyway. A formula instrument is $z_i = f_i(g, w)$ for a known function $f_i$. Its expected value $\mu_i = E[z_i \mid w]$ is its average over the shock draws that could have occurred, for the same unit with its $w$ fixed. It plays the role of the assignment probability in the stratified experiment. The recentered instrument $\tilde z_i = z_i - \mu_i$ averages zero over the draws for every unit, and it is valid, because by iterated expectations and @eq-ri-exog, $$ E[\tilde z_i \varepsilon_i] = E\big[\tilde z_i\, E[\varepsilon_i \mid g, w]\big] = E\big[\tilde z_i\, E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]\big] = E\big[E[\tilde z_i \mid w]\, E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]\big] = 0 . $$ Without recentering the same steps give $E[z_i \varepsilon_i] = E[\mu_i E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]]$, which is not zero when the expected instrument is correlated with the predictable part of the error. Computing $\mu_i$ requires the design: how the shocks could have been drawn. We redraw them from that design, or permute them if they are exchangeable, and average the formula over the draws. When the formula is linear in the shocks, this is the formula applied to the expected shocks. We can also keep $z_i$ as the instrument and control for $\mu_i$. In the population the two use the same variation, because the regression of $z_i$ on $\mu_i$ has slope one. In a sample the estimates differ slightly. Any recentered formula is valid, so we can pick the most precise. @borusyak-hull-2026 [Theorem 1] show that it starts from the best prediction of the treatment, recentered: $$ \tilde z = E[x \mid g, w] - E[x \mid w] . $$ {#eq-ri-optimal} Among recentered formulas it has the strongest first stage [@borusyak-hull-2026, Lemma 1]. The fully optimal instrument adds refinements that need a model of the error, and the authors drop them. When $x_i$ depends only on $(g, w)$, as eligibility does, the prediction is $x_i$ itself, and the instrument is the treatment minus its expected value. ## Shift-share as a formula instrument The Bartik instrument of @eq-shift-share-iv-1 is the linear formula $B_\ell = \sum_k s_{\ell k} g_k$, where $s_{\ell k}$ is region $\ell$'s employment share in industry $k$ and $g_k$ is the industry's shock. Suppose the shocks are exchangeable within period $t$, with mean $\bar g_t$, and let $S_\ell = \sum_k s_{\ell k}$ be the region's sum of shares. Then $$ \mu_\ell = S_\ell\, \bar g_t . $$ {#eq-ri-ss-mu} If the shares sum to one, $\mu_\ell = \bar g_t$ is the same for all regions and period effects absorb it, so Bartik is already recentered. If they are incomplete, as with manufacturing shares, regions with more manufacturing get a larger instrument in every draw, as stratum A got more treatment. Under the shock view Bartik is then biased unless we control for $S_\ell$ interacted with period [@borusyak-hull-jaravel-2022]. Under the share view, where the shares are as good as random given the controls [@goldsmith-pinkham-sorkin-swift-2020], Bartik is valid without it. ### A two-zone example Take two zones, P and Q, and three manufacturing industries in one period. Suppose we observe China shocks of 30, 0 and 0, in thousands of dollars of imports per worker, and that any reshuffling of these shocks across the industries was equally likely. Each industry is then the shocked one with probability 1/3, and the expected shock is $\bar g = 10$. Zone P has a share of 0.1 in each industry, so $S_P = 0.3$. Zone Q has a share of 0.1 in industry 3 only, so $S_Q = 0.1$. To keep the example short, suppose US import exposure equals $B_\ell$, so the instrument for exposure is $B_\ell - \mu_\ell$. The exposures in the three draws are: | Shocked industry | $B_P$ | $B_P - \mu_P$ | $B_Q$ | $B_Q - \mu_Q$ | |:----------------:|:-----:|:-------------:|:-----:|:-------------:| | 1 | 3 | 0 | 0 | −1 | | 2 | 3 | 0 | 0 | −1 | | 3 | 3 | 0 | 3 | 2 | By @eq-ri-ss-mu, $\mu_P = 0.3 \times 10 = 3$ and $\mu_Q = 0.1 \times 10 = 1$, the averages of each column of exposures. Let the change in the manufacturing employment share, in percentage points, be $$ y_\ell = -0.6 B_\ell - 10 S_\ell . $$ The first term is the effect of imports. The second is a decline that manufacturing-heavy zones have anyway, for example from automation. In two of the three draws P has exposure 3 and Q has none: $$ y_P - y_Q = -0.6 (3 - 0) - 10 (0.3 - 0.1) = -1.8 - 2 = -3.8 . $$ The raw slope is $-3.8/3 = -1.27 = -0.6 - 2/3$. P declines 2 points more than Q in every draw, and it also has more exposure in most draws, so the comparison counts the 2 points as an effect of imports. Pooling the three draws, the raw slope is −1.1. Each zone's $B_\ell - \mu_\ell$ averages zero over the draws, so it is uncorrelated with $S_\ell$, and as the instrument it gives exactly −0.6. Since $\mu_\ell = 10 S_\ell$, controlling for $S_\ell$ does the same. ### The formula Recentering is one difference between Bartik and @eq-ri-optimal. The other is the formula. Take two regions with half their employment in electronics, where only the first region's plants compete with Chinese imports. Bartik gives both half the electronics shock. The best predictor gives the first region half the shock and the second nothing. Once recentered both are valid, and the second has the stronger first stage. When the treatment really is shares times shocks, the best predictor is Bartik itself. The formula matters when the treatment has more structure: eligibility rules, transport networks, nonlinear indices. With heterogeneous effects, different instruments estimate different weighted averages [@borusyak-hull-2026, Proposition D1]. ## Simulation The aim is to compare a shock-only instrument with the recentered treatment when we know the true effect. There are 50 states and 10,000 people. Person $i$ lives in state $s(i)$ and has income $\text{inc}_i$, in multiples of the poverty line, drawn from a log-normal distribution with median 1.4. The shock is the states' policy: each state $k$ draws an eligibility threshold $T_k$ from $\{0.5, 1, 1.38, 2\}$, each value with probability 1/4, independently across states. Let $\alpha_k \sim N(0, 0.3^2)$ be a state effect and $\nu_i \sim N(0, 1)$ an individual error. Eligibility and the outcome are $$ x_i = 1[\text{inc}_i < T_{s(i)}], \qquad y_i = 0.3\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i = -0.5 \log \text{inc}_i + \alpha_{s(i)} + \nu_i . $$ {#eq-ri-dgp} The true effect is 0.3. The shocks $g$ are the 50 thresholds, and $w$ is the incomes and states. Poorer people are more often eligible and have higher errors, so OLS is biased upward. The thresholds are drawn independently of incomes and errors, so @eq-ri-exog holds. Expected eligibility $\mu_i$ is the share of the four thresholds above person $i$'s income: 1 below 0.5, 0.75 between 0.5 and 1, 0.5 between 1 and 1.38, 0.25 between 1.38 and 2, and 0 above 2. Income plays the role of the stratum. A person with income 1.2 has $\mu_i = 0.5$, and their recentered treatment $x_i - \mu_i$ is 0.5 if their state drew 1.38 or 2 and −0.5 if it drew 0.5 or 1, with equal chance whatever their error. People below 0.5 or above 2 always have zero and carry no identifying variation. We compare four estimators, all with standard errors clustered by state. 1. OLS of $y_i$ on $x_i$. It is biased. 2. The simulated instrument of @currie-gruber-1996. Each state's rules are applied to one fixed national sample, here all 10,000 people, and the share who would be eligible is the state's instrument. It measures the generosity of the rules and not the composition of the state's residents. It is valid. 3. The recentered treatment, instrumenting $x_i$ with $x_i - \mu_i$. It is valid. 4. OLS of $y_i$ on $x_i$ and $\mu_i$. Instrumenting $x_i$ with $x_i - \mu_i$ while controlling for $\mu_i$ reduces to this regression, because $x_i - \mu_i$ and $\mu_i$ add up to $x_i$ [@borusyak-hull-2026, footnote 8]. It is valid. The Monte Carlo is design-based. The people, their incomes, states and errors are fixed, and each of 1,000 replications draws new thresholds for the 50 states, which is the only randomness the identifying assumption allows. ::: {#cell-ri-mc .cell cache='true' execution_count=2} ``` {.julia .cell-code} people = CSV.read("data/recenter_people.csv", DataFrame) draws = Matrix(CSV.read("data/recenter_policy_draws.csv", DataFrame)[:, 2:end]) pool = [0.5, 1.0, 1.38, 2.0] beta_true = 0.3 mu = [mean(v .< pool) for v in people.income] # expected eligibility gener = [mean(people.income .< t) for t in pool] # state generosity function coef_x(f) i = findfirst(==("x"), coefnames(f)) return coef(f)[i], stderror(f)[i] end const CL = Vcov.cluster(:state) function one_draw(r) thr = draws[r, people.state] d = copy(people) d.x = Float64.(d.income .< thr) d.y = beta_true .* d.x .+ d.eps d.z_sim = gener[[findfirst(==(t), pool) for t in thr]] d.z_rc = d.x .- mu d.mu = mu fits = (feols(d, @formula(y ~ x), vcov = CL), feiv(d, @formula(y ~ 1), endo = :x, inst = :z_sim, vcov_type = CL), feiv(d, @formula(y ~ 1), endo = :x, inst = :z_rc, vcov_type = CL), feols(d, @formula(y ~ x + mu), vcov = CL)) r2 = [NaN, cor(d.x, d.z_sim)^2, cor(d.x, d.z_rc)^2, NaN] return [collect(coef_x(f)) for f in fits], r2 end R = size(draws, 1) est = zeros(R, 4); se = zeros(R, 4); r2 = zeros(R, 4) Threads.@threads for r in 1:R # one slot per draw, race-free cs, r2[r, :] = one_draw(r) for j in 1:4; est[r, j], se[r, j] = cs[j]; end end DataFrame(estimator = ["OLS", "Simulated instrument", "Recentered treatment", "OLS controlling for mu"], mean = round.(vec(mean(est, dims = 1)), digits = 3), sd = round.(vec(std(est, dims = 1)), digits = 3), coverage = round.(vec(mean(abs.(est .- beta_true) .<= 1.96 .* se, dims = 1)), digits = 3), first_stage_R2 = round.(vec(mean(r2, dims = 1)), digits = 3)) ``` ::: {#ri-mc .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

OLS averages 0.637, and its intervals never contain 0.3. The three other estimators are centred on 0.3, with coverage of 92.7% to 93.7%, slightly below 95% with 50 clusters. The simulated instrument has a standard deviation of 0.167 and a first-stage $R^2$ of 0.26, because it is the same for everyone in a state. The recentered treatment also uses the variation within states, among people whose eligibility depends on the threshold. Its standard deviation is 0.086, half as large, with an $R^2$ of 0.59, and its controlled form has 0.080. In real data, @borusyak-hull-2026 instrument Medicaid eligibility in the 2014 ACA expansion with actual minus expected eligibility, treating expansion as random within the governor's party. Over the simulated instrument the first-stage partial $R^2$ rises from 0.01 to 0.80, and the standard error on crowd-out falls by 44%. Most of the gain comes from the 18% of the sample whose eligibility the expansion could change. ## The China shock In ADH the shocks are the growth of Chinese imports into eight other high-income countries, per US worker, in 397 manufacturing industries over 1990–2000 and 2000–2007. ADH argue they are exogenous because the growth came from China's side, through reform, rising productivity and WTO accession. The argument is weaker for demand or technology shocks shared by all rich countries, and the identifying variation is concentrated in a few industries such as computers, toys and audio equipment [@goldsmith-pinkham-sorkin-swift-2020]. The treatment, US import exposure per worker, is shares times US import growth. Replacing US imports with the other-country shocks gives the prediction, which is the Bartik instrument itself. So the formula-instrument approach keeps the instrument and changes the control. The shares, lagged employment shares in the 722 commuting zones, are incomplete, so $\mu_\ell$ varies across zones. Its form depends on the shock design. - Design 1: the 397 shocks are exchangeable within each period. Every industry has the same expected shock, the period mean $\bar g_t$, which is 4.8 in the first period and 17.3 in the second, and $\mu_\ell = S_\ell \bar g_t$. - Design 2: the shocks are exchangeable only within each of the 20 two-digit SIC sectors in each period. Each industry's expected shock is its sector's mean $\bar g_{mt}$, and $\mu_\ell = \sum_m S_{\ell m} \bar g_{mt}$, where $S_{\ell m}$ is the zone's share in sector $m$. A zone heavy in electronics is then expected to receive a large instrument. ADH control for the start-of-period manufacturing share with one coefficient for both periods, which approximates design 1's $\mu_\ell$. The second row drops that control, so nothing recenters the instrument. All fits use ADH's other controls, census-division effects, population weights and standard errors clustered by state, with the GPSS replication files. ::: {#cell-ri-adh .cell cache='true' execution_count=3} ``` {.julia .cell-code} adh = CSV.read("data/adh_master.csv", DataFrame) tr = CSV.read("data/adh_shares_triplets.csv", DataFrame) shk = CSV.read("data/adh_shocks.csv", DataFrame) function by_row(v) # sum over industries, by zone out = zeros(nrow(adh)) for (r, x) in zip(tr.row, v); out[r] += x; end return out end sector = string.(shk.sic87dd .÷ 100, " ", shk.year) g_bar_m = Dict(s => mean(shk.g[sector .== s]) for s in unique(sector)) adh.B = by_row(tr.share .* shk.g[tr.col]) adh.S = by_row(tr.share) adh.S_t2 = adh.S .* adh.t2 adh.t2n = Float64.(adh.t2) adh.mu2 = by_row(tr.share .* [g_bar_m[sector[c]] for c in tr.col]) controls = term(:l_sh_popedu_c) + term(:l_sh_popfborn) + term(:l_sh_empl_f) + term(:l_sh_routine33) + term(:l_task_outsource) + term(:t2n) + fe(:division) function iv(extra) rhs = isempty(extra) ? controls : sum(term.(extra)) + controls feiv(adh, term(:d_sh_empl_mfg) ~ rhs, endo = :shock, inst = :B, weights = :weights, vcov_type = Vcov.cluster(:statefip)) end fits = ["Bartik, ADH controls" => iv([:l_shind_manuf_cbp]), "Bartik, no manufacturing control" => iv(Symbol[]), "Bartik, design 1 mu (S x period)" => iv([:S, :S_t2]), "Bartik, design 2 mu (sector means)" => iv([:mu2])] DataFrame(specification = first.(fits), estimate = [round(coef(f)[1], digits = 3) for f in last.(fits)], se = [round(stderror(f)[1], digits = 3) for f in last.(fits)]) ``` ::: {#ri-adh .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The first row reproduces ADH's −0.596: an increase in import exposure of \$1,000 per worker over a decade lowers the manufacturing employment share by about 0.6 percentage points. Without the manufacturing-share control the estimate is −0.712. Controlling for design 1's $\mu_\ell$ lowers the estimate to −0.267 (0.087). ADH's control is close to $S_\ell$, with a correlation of 0.92, but the slope of $\mu_\ell$ on $S_\ell$ is the mean shock, which more than triples between periods, and one coefficient cannot match both. So ADH's estimate still compares manufacturing-heavy zones in the second period, when they get a much larger instrument whichever industries China hit. Design 2 also removes the comparison across sectors, such as electronics and toys against food and paper, and the estimate falls to −0.144 (0.117). Whether the removed comparisons are confounded is the substantive question. If manufacturing-heavy zones declined faster in the 2000s for other reasons, such as automation, the design 1 control is needed and ADH overstate the effect. But the average shock is itself part of the China shock, since Chinese imports rose across nearly all of manufacturing. Designs 1 and 2 use only the variation in which industries China hit harder than average, so they cannot measure an effect that works through manufacturing as a whole. ADH's −0.596 does use it, and it is valid if the shares are exogenous given the controls. The data cannot tell us which assumption holds. Every estimate is negative, and recentering shows how much of the size depends on the assumption. ## Spillovers: deworming @miguel-kremer-2004 study a deworming programme in 75 primary schools in Busia, Kenya, assigned in three groups of 25 that started treatment in different years. Worms spread between children, so treating one school can lower infection at schools nearby. To measure this, they count the pupils at treated schools within 3 km of each school, and they control for the total number of pupils within 3 km. Let $D_j$ be 1 if school $j$ is treated, $n_j$ its number of pupils, $p_j$ the probability that it is treated, and $j \sim i$ mean that $j$ is another school within 3 km of school $i$. The spillover exposure of school $i$ and its expected value are $$ x_i = \sum_{j \sim i} n_j D_j, \qquad \mu_i = \sum_{j \sim i} n_j p_j . $$ {#eq-ri-spill} The shocks are the assignments, and $w$ is the locations and pupil counts. Assignment is random, but a school in a dense area has more treated neighbours in every draw. If density also affects the outcome, through crowding or sanitation, exposure is correlated with the error. In the first year one third of the schools were treated, so $p_j = 1/3$ and $\mu_i$ is one third of the total pupils within 3 km. Miguel and Kremer's control is therefore the recentering. If the probability differed across schools, for example by stratum, the control would have to be $\mu_i$ and not the total pupils. The exposure is the treatment itself, so the estimator is OLS controlling for $\mu_i$, as estimator 4 above. A second simulation checks this. We place 75 schools in a 30 km by 30 km district, half around a town and half spread over the rest, with about 400 pupils each. In each draw exactly 25 schools are treated, so $p_j = 1/3$. Let $N_i$ be the total pupils at other schools within 3 km and $\eta_i \sim N(0, 0.05^2)$ a school error. The outcome, school participation, is $$ y_i = 0.05 D_i + 0.03 x_i - 0.02 N_i + \eta_i , $$ {#eq-ri-spill-dgp} with $x_i$ and $N_i$ in thousands of pupils. Treatment raises participation by 5 points at the school and by 3 points per thousand treated pupils nearby, and schools in dense areas have lower participation for other reasons. As before, only the assignment is redrawn across 1,000 replications. We regress $y_i$ on $D_i$ and on (a) $x_i$, (b) $x_i - \mu_i$, or (c) $x_i$ and $N_i$, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. ::: {#cell-ri-deworm .cell cache='true' execution_count=4} ``` {.julia .cell-code} schools = CSV.read("data/deworm_schools.csv", DataFrame) treat = Matrix(CSV.read("data/deworm_draws.csv", DataFrame)[:, 2:end]) ns = nrow(schools) near = [i != j && hypot(schools.east[i] - schools.east[j], schools.north[i] - schools.north[j]) < 3 for i in 1:ns, j in 1:ns] # within 3 km N = near * schools.pupils ./ 1000 # total pupils nearby, thousands mu = N ./ 3 # expected treated pupils nearby function one_assign(r) D = Float64.(treat[r, :]) x = near * (schools.pupils .* D) ./ 1000 d = DataFrame(D = D, x = x, N = N, x_rc = x .- mu, y = 0.05 .* D .+ 0.03 .* x .- 0.02 .* N .+ schools.eta) fits = (feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x), vcov = Vcov.robust()), feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x_rc), vcov = Vcov.robust()), feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x + N), vcov = Vcov.robust())) return [(coef(f)[3], stderror(f)[3]) for f in fits] end R = size(treat, 1) dw_est = zeros(R, 3); dw_se = zeros(R, 3) Threads.@threads for r in 1:R # one slot per draw, race-free for (j, (b, s)) in enumerate(one_assign(r)) dw_est[r, j], dw_se[r, j] = b, s end end DataFrame(estimator = ["(a) Exposure, no control", "(b) Recentered exposure", "(c) Exposure, control for nearby pupils"], mean = round.(vec(mean(dw_est, dims = 1)), digits = 3), sd = round.(vec(std(dw_est, dims = 1)), digits = 3), coverage = round.(vec(mean(abs.(dw_est .- 0.03) .<= 1.96 .* dw_se, dims = 1)), digits = 3)) ``` ::: {#ri-deworm .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

Regressing on $x_i - \mu_i$ alone leaves $-0.02 N_i$ in the error, so its standard deviation is 0.038, about twice the 0.020 of (c). Neighbouring schools share that error and the same treated schools, so the robust intervals of (b) contain 0.03 only 43% of the time. With the control the remaining error is independent across schools, and coverage is 92%. ### A two-school example Take two untreated schools, A and B, and three other schools, 1, 2 and 3, with 400 pupils each. Exactly one of the three is treated, each with probability 1/3. Town school A has all three within 3 km, so $N_A = 1.2$ thousand. Rural school B has only school 3 nearby, so $N_B = 0.4$. The exposures in the three draws are: | Treated school | $x_A$ | $x_A - \mu_A$ | $x_B$ | $x_B - \mu_B$ | |:--------------:|:-----:|:-------------:|:-----:|:-------------:| | 1 | 0.4 | 0 | 0 | −0.133 | | 2 | 0.4 | 0 | 0 | −0.133 | | 3 | 0.4 | 0 | 0.4 | 0.267 | The expected exposures are $\mu_A = 0.4$ and $\mu_B = 0.133$, the pupils nearby times 1/3. In two of the three draws A has one treated neighbour and B has none, and with $\eta_i$ set to zero @eq-ri-spill-dgp gives $$ y_A - y_B = 0.03 (0.4 - 0) - 0.02 (1.2 - 0.4) = 0.012 - 0.016 = -0.004 . $$ The raw slope is $-0.004/0.4 = -0.01$, against a true 0.03. A has more pupils nearby, which lowers its participation in every draw, and more exposure in most draws, so the comparison counts the density gap as spillover. Pooling the three draws, the raw slope is 0. The recentered exposure is always 0 for A and averages zero for B, so it is uncorrelated with $N_i$, and with any other fixed characteristic of a school, and as the instrument it gives exactly 0.03. ## Summary A treatment built from random shocks and fixed exposure is not random, for the same reason a stratified assignment is not: some units expect more treatment in every draw. Subtracting the expected treatment, computed from the formula and the shock design, or controlling for it, leaves only the variation from the draw. For Bartik with manufacturing shares, the expected instrument is the sum of shares times the period's mean shock, and controlling for it moves the ADH estimate from −0.60 to −0.27. For spillovers it is the treatment probability times nearby pupils, the control Miguel and Kremer used. For the shift-share construction, the share and shock views, and inference, see the previous chapter, [Shift-Share Instrumental Variables](shift-share-iv.qmd).
